## Two models, same accuracy {#motivation}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Model A: misses 60 good hires, flags 40 bad ones.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
Model B: misses 40 good hires, flags 60 bad ones.
:::
::::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.keyidea}
[Key idea]{.label}
Same accuracy, different consequences. Accuracy cannot tell them apart.
:::
:::

## What a decision needs {#definition}

::: {.definition}
[Definition]{.label}
A *decision rule* maps a signal $s$ to an action $a = \delta(s)$. A *loss*
$L(a, y)$ says what it costs to take action $a$ when the truth is $y$.
:::

::: {.example}
[Example]{.label}
Screening applicants: $a \in \{\text{interview}, \text{reject}\}$, and
$L(\text{reject}, \text{qualified})$ is the cost of missing a good hire.
:::

## Why prediction is not decision {#build}

- A model gives you a posterior $\hat p(y \mid x)$.
- A decision needs a loss $L(a, y)$.
- Only together do they give an action.

::: {.fragment}
$$a^\star = \argmin_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \E\big[L(a, y) \mid s\big]$$
:::

::: {.notes}
The list stages itself; `incremental: true` is set by the format. Pause on the
second bullet and ask where the loss comes from.
:::

## Worked example: the hiring screen {#worked}

<ol class="steps">
<li>Write the decision problem: choose $a$ to minimize expected loss.</li>
<li>Substitute the posterior: $\E[L(a, y) \mid s]$.</li>
<li>Minimize over the two actions.</li>
<li>Read the threshold off the loss ratio: $\tau = 1/(1 + c_{FN}/c_{FP})$.</li>
</ol>

::: {.aside-note}
The threshold is a loss ratio and nothing else.
:::

::: {.with-previous}
[Threshold Formula]{.jump target="ap-threshold"}
:::

## The threshold moves {auto-animate="true" #thr1}

::: {.hero}
$\tau = 0.50$
:::

Equal costs.

## The threshold moves {auto-animate="true" #thr2}

::: {.hero}
$\tau = 0.09$
:::

A missed hire costs ten times a wasted interview.

## Appendix {.appendix-break background-color="var(--appendix-ground)"}

## Where the threshold formula comes from {.appendix #ap-threshold}

<ol class="steps">
<li>Set the two expected losses equal at the indifference point.</li>
<li>Solve for the posterior probability that makes them equal.</li>
<li>Read $\tau = 1/(1 + c_{FN}/c_{FP})$ off the result.</li>
</ol>
